news.2026-10-27-serbie-liste-etudiants-v: In Serbia, the student movement beats Vučić in parliamentary elections after fourteen years in power
The Student List won the snap parliamentary election on 25 October and Aleksandar Vučić conceded defeat. It should hold a majority in Parliament on its own.
On 25 October the Student List won Serbia's snap parliamentary election, and Aleksandar Vučić, in power for fourteen years, conceded defeat: “The Student List has won” [1][2].

According to still-preliminary results from the Electoral Commission (8,077 of 8,392 polling stations counted), the Student List took 52.54% of the vote, against 39.29% for Vučić's list; Euronews gives a slightly different figure for the latter [1][2]. Vučić himself estimates the students will have between 135 and 140 of the 250 seats, and his camp about 105 [2].

The movement grew out of nearly two years of youth-led protests, after 16 people died when the canopy of the Novi Sad railway station collapsed in 2024. Vučić blamed independent media and foreign interference; the students have not yet named a prime minister [2][3].
Key point: a list carried by students, none of whom was a candidate, has just stripped of its majority a leader who had held Serbia for fourteen years [1][2].

The hard part begins: the new power must form a government, choose a prime minister and say what it will do with the budget and the big contracts. The sources consulted do not yet detail its economic programme, and the results are not final [2].

Serbia is a European country that borders several EU members. What the new government does (budget, relations with Brussels and with Moscow) will weigh on the stability of the Balkans and on companies investing there.

news.2026-10-27-bresil-lula-reelu-bourse: Lula re-elected for a fourth term: Brazil's stock market plunges almost 14% in one session
Markets had bet on a win for Flávio Bolsonaro. Lula won by about 4.4 million votes, and stocks and the currency fell on Monday.

On 25 October Lula won the runoff with 51.79% of the vote against 48.21% for Flávio Bolsonaro, a lead of about 4.4 million votes. His opponent refuses to recognise the result and wants to ask the courts to annul it [1].

On Monday 26 October the Ibovespa, the São Paulo stock index, lost as much as 17% during the session before closing down 13.9%, while the real, Brazil's currency, plunged against the dollar [2][3]. Sources differ on the exact size of the real's fall.
According to Bloomberg, investors had positioned heavily for a Bolsonaro win; they also fear higher public spending, with the deficit close to 10% of GDP after pre-election spending [2][4].
Key point: it is not only the election that sank the stock market, it is the surprise: the market had bet on the other camp [2][4].

When a currency falls, imported goods (fuel, fertiliser, wheat) cost more in reais, and dollar debts become heavier. Conversely, exporters of soy, meat or ore gain. It remains to be seen whether Flávio Bolsonaro's court challenge, seen as unlikely to succeed given the margin, prolongs the turbulence [1].

Brazil is a major supplier of soy, coffee and meat. A falling currency makes its products cheaper for foreign buyers, and big funds holding Brazilian shares, including in European investments, may have lost value.

news.2026-10-27-cisjordanie-hebron-famil: In Hebron, the Israeli army displaces hundreds of families after two soldiers are killed, on the eve of elections
After an attack on a checkpoint on 23 October, the army sealed off the city and removed families from a neighbourhood; figures range from 150 families to 2,000 people. Israel votes on the 27th.
On 23 October two Israeli soldiers were killed at a checkpoint near Hebron, in the West Bank; the army launched a large operation in the city, home to about 200,000 people [1][2][3].

Defence Minister Israel Katz speaks of about 2,000 people displaced as of Saturday evening; the municipality counts 370 families, the governor about 150 and the mayor about 250 [1][2]. Governor Khaled Dudin denounces collective punishment and a state of emergency has been declared in the province [2].

Buildings near the site of the attack have been demolished, and Benjamin Netanyahu announced that more would be. The operation comes days before a tightly contested election, which Hebron's mayor calls a political move [3].
Key point: the numbers of displaced people vary by a factor of up to ten depending on who gives them, a sign that the situation on the ground is still unclear [1][2].

Israel votes on 27 October, and the latest polls point to a deadlock: neither Netanyahu's bloc nor the opposition would reach the 61-seat majority, which makes small parties decisive [4]. The economic cost of a prolonged conflict is one of the campaign's big themes [4].

Violence in the West Bank and the Israeli campaign feed uncertainty across the region, and therefore oil prices and shipping insurance. The outcome of the vote will shape what happens next in the Gaza war and relations with Iran.

news.2026-10-27-niger-penurie-carburant-: Niger produces oil but is short of petrol: Niamey bans fuel exports
Queues have appeared at the capital's filling stations. An order dated 12 October bans exports of diesel and petrol unless authorised.

On 12 October the Trade Minister signed an order banning exports of diesel and “premium” petrol; only the state companies SONIDEP and SORAZ may sell a surplus abroad, with the minister's approval for each cargo [1][2].
On 18 October long queues formed at Niamey's filling stations; the cheaper smuggled Nigerian fuel has almost disappeared [3].

The country extracts about 90,000 barrels of crude a day at Agadem, but its Zinder refinery processes only about 20,000, too little for national demand; cross-debts between the state, the oil companies and the power utility Nigelec complicate matters [2][3].
Key point: a country that has oil can still run out of petrol if it lacks the refineries to process it [2].

Banning exports keeps fuel in the country but does not create any: the underlying problem is the lack of refining capacity and the debts. A fuel shortage can also hamper transport, mines and electricity, and the business press links it to disruption from the conflict with Iran [1][3].
Niger is also a uranium country. A country short of fuel struggles to keep its trucks and mines running, which can delay some ore deliveries [3].

news.2026-10-27-mozambique-etat-vingt-po: Mozambique wants to become a 20% shareholder in all its big mines
President Daniel Chapo announced on 20 October that a state company would hold 20% of mining projects, above the 15% already set by the June law.

On 20 October, in Nacala, President Daniel Chapo announced that a state-owned national mining company would take 20% of mining projects, whereas the law signed on 3 June already provides for a 15% stake [1][2].
At the same conference the government signed memorandums of understanding covering $4.2 billion of ore-processing projects on site [2].

The rules remain unclear: it is not known which projects will be covered, whether existing mines are included, or how the law's 15% and the announced 20% fit together. One source notes that the official text of the law was not consulted, so exact figures should be treated with caution [3].
Key point: Mozambique wants to keep a larger share of its minerals and process part of them at home, rather than export everything raw [1][2].

A 20% stake does not mean 20% of revenue: the state receives a share of the profits, but sometimes must also pay its share of the costs. For mining groups, everything depends on the details of the text, hence investors' attention [3].
The minerals go into batteries, devices and industrial parts. If conditions become stricter for mining groups, some projects may cost more or be delayed, which can end up weighing on prices.

news.2026-10-27-mexique-camionneurs-bloq: Mexico: truckers and farmers block highways “indefinitely” to protest insecurity and tolls
Since 26 October, blockades have hit the approaches to Mexico City, Veracruz and Oaxaca. Protesters demand security, an end to extortion and lighter tolls.

Since Monday 26 October, truckers and farmers have been blocking roads in about twenty states, notably at the entrances to the capital and in the states of Veracruz and Oaxaca; organisers speak of an “indefinite” action [1][2].

They demand more security against theft, kidnapping and extortion on the roads, an end to the protection money demanded by criminal groups, and tolls and taxes they consider too heavy for dangerous roads; Highway 135D between Tehuacán and Oaxaca was fully closed [1][2][3].

The Interior Ministry says most organisations accepted a round of talks, but no deal had been announced; the Conatram confederation says none of its members is taking part, and sources contradict each other on who is really blocking [1][3].
Key point: the blockade targets the roads along which goods travel, and organisers say it has no end date [1][2].

The movement stems from very concrete insecurity on the roads, which carriers say they face every day, more than from a political slogan. If talks fail, the blockade could last, as organisers promise [1][2].
Mexico makes and exports many products that travel by road. A long blockade can delay deliveries and raise the price of some goods.

news.2026-10-27-asean-reseau-electrique-: Southeast Asia: Singapore wants to link countries with undersea power cables, with Laos at the centre
For its 2027 ASEAN chairmanship, Singapore wants common rules for trading electricity through undersea cables. Laos, rich in dams, is the central link.
Singapore, which will chair ASEAN in 2027, wants to advance the “ASEAN Power Grid”, with a common framework for undersea power cables; the aim is for member states to adopt it in 2027 [1][2].

Today ASEAN has no single set of rules for selling electricity from one country to another, and it is not clear who must inspect, maintain or repair these cables; investors, who take 20 to 30 years to recoup their money, want stability [1].

Laos is at the heart of the project: the Laos–Thailand–Malaysia–Singapore link is to grow from 100 to 200 megawatts [1]. Singapore and Laos also signed a carbon-credit agreement on 4 September, with 58 pre-approved methodologies, including 5% of proceeds paid to Laos for climate adaptation [3]. Thailand takes over the chair in 2028 [4].
Key point: Singapore, a small island with no rivers or dams, is looking to buy clean electricity from neighbours such as Laos [1][3].

For this to work, common rules are needed on prices, ownership and cable repair, and guarantees for investors. Laotian dams produce a lot of electricity, but Laos can only sell it if the lines and rules keep pace [1][3].
Data centres and factories in Southeast Asia use more and more electricity. The cost of energy in this region influences the price of chips, phones and products made there.

news.2026-10-27-ebola-rdc-deuxieme-plus-: Ebola in DR Congo: nearly 10,000 confirmed cases, the second-largest outbreak ever recorded
Starting in Ituri, the outbreak caused by the Bundibugyo virus has killed 4,687 people according to the latest European tally. Cases are also reported in Kenya and Nigeria.

As of 21 October, DR Congo had 9,704 confirmed Ebola cases, including 4,687 deaths, according to the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC); Ituri is the hardest-hit province, with 7,003 cases and 3,242 deaths in 28 of its 36 health zones [1].
The US CDC reported 9,235 confirmed cases on 15 October and called it the second-largest Ebola outbreak ever recorded [2]. It is caused by the Bundibugyo virus [1].

The virus has crossed borders: Kenya has 9 confirmed cases, all linked to a first imported case, and Nigeria reported a case on 20 October; four cases have been evacuated or imported to Europe since May. Uganda's figures are disputed depending on the source [1].
Key point: the official toll is approaching 10,000 confirmed cases, and the epidemic is not confined to a single region of the country [1][2].

Epidemics weigh on the economy: schools and markets closed, travellers turned back at borders, mines and transport slowed in a region already weakened by conflict. The two sources do not use the same reporting date, so exact figures may differ [1][2].

The risk for France remains limited, but the cases evacuated to Europe show that countries are following the situation closely. For the economy, a long epidemic in DR Congo, the world's top cobalt producer, could hamper ore transport.
